newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine tax confusion keeps investors guessing.
newsitem.headline: Argentine tax confusion keeps investors guessing.

text.p: The constant chopping and changing of Argentine taxes is confusing taxpayers, hampering recovery and clouding the horizon for business which is urging fiscal stability to plan investments, economic analysts say.

"Neither people nor businesses can foresee how much tax they are going to have to pay nor when, since it's changing all the time," said Ines Piccinino, an economist for private analysts Asesores Economicos.
This instability is the product of government efforts to curb a budget deficit it acknowledges may hit at least $5 billion this year, against $2.5 billion agreed with the International Monetary Fund.
In two years the government has hiked the value added tax to 21 percent from 18 percent and promised to reduce it to 20 percent next year.
As for the personal wealth tax, it has been doubled to 1.0 percent before going back down again to 0.5 percent. The government also expanded the wealth tax base to $102,300 from $100,000.

It has tinkered with the tariff regime, eliminating the tax-free status of capital goods imports, while reducing payroll taxes, slapping a 14 percent tax on the hitherto tax-free food vouchers and slashing family allowance benefits.

Now influential ruling party congressmen could complicate the tax structure by seeking to reintroduce an internal tax on cola drinks that was eliminated three months ago and adding five percentage points on all import tariffs, except on goods from Argentina's Mercosur trade-bloc partners Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.

As the Peronist government negotiates with legislators and governors, offering the provinces a share of an 10 percent hike in income tax in exchange for keeping all revenue from new fuel taxes, budget-watchers complain they have a hard time keeping up with the changes.

"These successive alterations in the tax package, together with announcements by the authorities which are subsequently denied or changed, create a climate of discontent," commented economist Rodolfo Rossi, a former Central Bank president.

The Argentine Chamber of Commerce's vice-President Silvia Macchiavello said sales fell between 10 and 15 percent last month "because of the uncertainty generated by tax announcements that never get clearly defined."
One upside is that the threat of new taxes on diesel vehicles drove up diesel car sales.
"In the last week of August there was incredible growth in purchases of trucks and buses," said Luis Katz, a director of the auto manufacturers' body ADEFA.

But according to analyst Piccinino, the winners from this situation are few and far between. "And the worst thing is that there is a high probability that these changes in taxes will carry on, so the level of uncertainty will stay high."
